# RaftCore v1.0.0

The first stable release of **RaftCore**, a transport-agnostic C++23 implementation of the Raft consensus algorithm's core — leader election and log replication — built on this project's own container and callable libraries.

## Highlights

- Pure consensus core — no sockets, threads, clocks, or disk I/O. You supply the `Transport`, `Storage`, `PersistentState`, and `RandomSource`; RaftCore supplies the protocol.
- Leader election: `RequestVote` handling, per-term vote tracking, randomized election timeouts, and step-down on any higher term observed.
- Log replication: `AppendEntries` handling with prev-log consistency checks, conflict truncation, duplicate-entry skipping, and per-peer `nextIndex`/`matchIndex` tracking.
- Commit-index advancement by majority `matchIndex`, with `commitIndex`/`lastApplied` tracked on `NodeState`.
- Tick-driven timing: `RaftNode::tick()` drives election timeouts and leader heartbeats — no wall clock, so runs are fully deterministic under test.
- Pluggable interfaces: `Transport`, `Storage`, `PersistentState`, `RandomSource`, and `StateMachine`.
- `SystemRandomSource` included; inject a scripted or fake `RandomSource` for deterministic elections.
- `[[nodiscard]] Status` on every fallible call (`OK`, `IO_ERROR`, `NOT_FOUND`, `OUT_OF_MEMORY`, `PARSE_ERROR`) — storage and transport failures propagate instead of being swallowed.
- `takeLastAsyncError()` surfaces failures that occur inside reply callbacks, which can't return a `Status` to the caller.
- Asynchronous reply callbacks via `MoveOnlyFunction`, so a callback can own move-only state.
- Leader-only state (`nextIndex`/`matchIndex`) exists only while the node is Leader, via `std::optional`.
- Built directly on `VectorPro`, `HashMapPro`, and `FunctionPro`.

## Performance

The hot paths are designed around avoiding unnecessary allocation, copying, and work:

- Role, term, commit-index, and self-id accessors are single-load reads — sub-nanosecond to ~2 ns per call.
- Stale-term `AppendEntries` and `RequestVote` are rejected immediately, before touching the log.
- Leader-only state is allocated once on `becomeLeader()` and torn down on step-down, not carried by every node.
- `LogEntry` and `AppendEntriesArgs` are movable, so batches of entries can be handed to `Transport` without a deep copy.
- Replication to a peer sends only the entries past that peer's `nextIndex`, not the whole log.
- Commit advancement stops at the highest index a majority has replicated, rather than checking every index.

## Benchmarks

RaftCore has no natural drop-in standard-library equivalent to benchmark against (there's no `std::` consensus library) --
these are absolute measurements, not a comparison. Figures below are at
1M iterations; full results across every subsystem and scale:
`benchmarks/baselines/v1.0.0/v1.0.0.md`.

| Test                                | 1M       |
|-------------------------------------|----------|
| Leader State (`leaderState` access) | 873.36 µs |
| Term (`currentTerm` access)         | 1.40 ms  |
| AppendEntries Heartbeat             | 22.51 ms |
| AppendEntries Append                | 55.01 ms |
| RequestVote Grant                   | 42.76 ms |
| Leader Reply Commit                 | 117.41 ms |
| Become Leader                       | 249.31 ms |
| Election Round                      | 722.50 ms |
| Commit Advance (1000-entry log)     | 74.02 s  |

A few things worth calling out honestly:

- **Accessors are effectively free**: `role`, `commitIndex`, and `selfId` each cost ~0.84 ms per 1M calls (under 1 ns per call).
- **Moving entries is far cheaper than copying them**: `Args Mv 100` takes 10.68 ms versus 2.36 s for `Args Cp 100` (roughly 220x), and `Entry Mv 256` takes 315.29 µs versus 14.15 ms for `Entry Cp 256` (roughly 45x). Move entries wherever you hand them off.
- **Cost scales linearly with peer count**: `Lead 100` takes 8.13 s versus 156.94 ms for `Lead 2` (about 52x for 50x the peers), and `Beat 100` is 3.51 s versus 70.03 ms for `Beat 2`. Expected, since leader-side work is one send per peer, but worth knowing before running a very large cluster.
- **Commit advancement with a long log is the single most expensive operation measured**, and by a wide margin -- `Commit 1000` at 1M iterations takes 74.02 s versus 114.35 ms for `Commit 1`, roughly a 650x gap for 1000x the log length. Expected, given that each advance scans downward from the log tail toward `commitIndex`, doing an `entryAt` lookup plus a sweep over every peer's `matchIndex` per candidate, but worth knowing before letting a large uncommitted gap build up on a latency-sensitive path.
- **`SystemRandomSource` construction is expensive** (2.67 s per 1M constructions, ~2.7 µs each, from seeding via `std::random_device`) while drawing from one is cheap (~3 ms per 1M calls). Construct it once and reuse it.

## Testing

The project includes a comprehensive test suite (341 tests) covering:

- Unit-level correctness for `NodeState`, election logic, and replication logic in isolation
- Cross-component integration: single-node election, multi-node log replication, and restart recovery against persisted state
- Lifecycle invariants: legal role transitions, `Status` propagation from storage and transport failures, and term monotonicity
- Concurrency and fault scenarios: split votes, partitioned leaders, leader crash during replication, and log conflict resolution
- Fuzzing: two ClusterFuzzLite harnesses (`fuzz_raft_rpc`, `fuzz_raft_cluster`) feed arbitrary operation sequences to a node and a cluster, checking invariants after every operation (terms and commit index never decrease, no vote granted to a stale term, no vote changed within a term)
- A regression suite that compares benchmark runs against the saved `v1.0.0` baseline
- A runnable examples suite (quickstart, patterns, advanced, integration, and misuse cases) that doubles as usage documentation

## Code Coverage

The current test suite achieves:

- **89.1% line coverage** (262 / 294 lines)
- **90.2% function coverage** (37 / 41 functions)

| Directory                | Line Coverage    | Function Coverage |
|--------------------------|------------------|-------------------|
| `src/RaftCore/Core`      | 89.0% (258/290)  | 89.2% (33/37)     |
| `include/RaftCore/Interfaces` | 100.0% (4/4) | 100.0% (4/4)      |

Coverage reports exclude test infrastructure and submodule dependencies
(`libs/internal/`), focusing on RaftCore's own implementation.
`Core`'s function coverage is the softest spot -- the four uncovered
functions are the `NodeState::log()` and `NodeState::leaderState()`
const accessors and both `RaftNode::state()` overloads. Worth a look
before the next release.

## Continuous Integration

Automated builds, tests, and checks are configured across:

- Multi-compiler builds: GCC and Clang on Linux, MSVC on Windows, and AppleClang on macOS, each in Debug and Release
- ASan/UBSan and a separate TSan job
- `clang-format` and `clang-tidy` checks on every push and pull request
- Code coverage collection, with submodule and test-infrastructure sources excluded from the measured result
- ClusterFuzzLite fuzzing on pull requests, plus a longer scheduled batch run
- CodeQL and OpenSSF Scorecard security analysis, both on a weekly schedule
- Conan and vcpkg packaging, each verified with a consumer smoke test against the built package
- Automatic Conan recipe, vcpkg port, and `CMakeLists.txt` version/hash bumps whenever a `v*` tag is pushed
- API documentation generated with Doxygen and published to GitHub Pages

## Release

This release represents the first stable version of RaftCore and establishes its consensus core, interface contracts, fuzzing and test coverage, and cross-platform build and packaging pipeline.

## Installation

Clone the repository and integrate RaftCore into your C++ project using the provided CMake configuration.

See the project documentation for build instructions, API usage, and integration details.
